papers.title: What message features influence the intention to share misinformation about COVID-19 on social media? The role of efficacy and novelty
papers.finding: Korean experiment (N=1,012) on how novelty and efficacy of misinformation affect sharing through emotion and credibility.

papers.title: Who spread COVID-19 (mis)information online? Differential informedness, psychological mechanisms, and intervention strategies
papers.finding: Chinese surveys: misinformed and uninformed people were more likely to spread misinformation; positive-emotion content spread more.

papers.why: Supports teaching students to seek news actively rather than rely on feeds or AI summaries.
papers.title: Social media may hinder learning about science; social media's role in learning about COVID-19
papers.finding: US two-wave panel. Getting news from social media fostered a news-finds-me belief, which left people less informed and more misinformed about COVID-19.

children.name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
children.blurb: Coaching students through primary sources means using a school configured AI tool as a question asking coach rather than an interpreter, so students still do the reading, reasoning, and writing themselves.

children.name: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
children.blurb: Historical role play with AI lets students interview or debate simulated historical figures, but only when every simulation is clearly labeled as a simulation and every quote or claim is checked against a real source.

children.name: Perspectives and Missing Voices
children.blurb: AI can help social studies students explore multiple perspectives on a historical event and help teachers identify groups that textbooks often leave out.

children.name: Why a Teacher Reads First
children.blurb: Before students see any AI output that describes people, events, or cultures, a teacher should read it first.

children.name: Current Events and Misinformation
children.blurb: Current events and misinformation is a teaching approach that uses AI tools to bring news into the classroom at multiple reading levels and to help students investigate false stories.

children.name: Civic Simulations, Debate, and Mock Trial
children.blurb: Civic simulations, debate, and mock trial let students practice civics rather than only read about it, with AI playing supporting roles such as constituents, opponents, witnesses, or economic actors.

children.name: Timelines, Maps, and Local History
children.blurb: Visual tools such as timelines and maps help students organize history in time and space, with AI assisting only with formatting and design while students decide what events matter and why.

children.name: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
children.blurb: AI can give world language students far more practice than a single class period allows, through conversation partners, writing feedback, and pronunciation tools.

children.name: Translation as a Lesson
children.blurb: Translation as a Lesson is a teaching approach in which students translate a passage themselves and then compare their work with a machine translation, such as one from Microsoft Translator, to find where meaning, tone, idiom, and accuracy succeed or fail.

children.name: Access for Every Student
children.blurb: Access for Every Student means using AI to make social studies content reachable for every learner, including students reading below grade level, English learners, and students with disabilities.

children.name: Heritage Speakers and Family Languages
children.blurb: Heritage speakers are students who already speak a language other than English at home, often fluently, but who may have had little practice reading and writing it.

children.name: Geography and Data
children.blurb: Geography and data work well together when AI helps students find public data sets and suggests questions, while students build their own maps to show patterns.

children.name: Planning and Assessment in These Subjects
children.blurb: In social studies, civics and world languages, teachers can use an approved AI tool to draft unit outlines, lesson sets, practice passages and quiz items, then check and edit everything before students see it.

sections.body: This part of school life covers social studies, civics and world languages, where students work with sources, perspectives, events and languages. The book describes AI answering questions in the voice of a historical figure, showing how different people might see the same event, giving language learners endless conversation practice, and letting a class explore economic or political choices through simulation. It also covers primary source coaching, historical role play, perspective taking and missing voices, current events and misinformation, civic simulations and debate, timelines and local history, and several uses in world languages. The risk is that AI produces fluent text that can include invented quotes, dates and sources, and in history and civics an invented quote attributed to a real person can distort the past. All of these uses depend on a teacher reading what the tool says before students rely on it.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works is a simple review practice that teachers actually follow, where any AI generated historical content, perspective or source is read by the teacher before students use it, simulations are labeled, and quotes are verified against real sources. A general policy on AI use is not enough on its own, because what counts is a routine applied lesson by lesson. What does not work is the convincing simulation, where a class interviews a simulated historical figure, students copy memorable quotes into essays, nobody checks whether the figure ever said them, and the invented history spreads without looking like a mistake at the time. The rule the book holds to is that a teacher reads first, and it notes that only one idea here carries strong evidence, so most should begin as small pilots.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a sequence from source work to classroom practice. A teacher would go to Coaching Students Through Primary Sources and Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation for the core routines, then to Perspectives and Missing Voices and Why a Teacher Reads First for the bias question that explains why every perspective tool needs a teacher reading first. Current Events and Misinformation, Civic Simulations, Debate, and Mock Trial, and Timelines, Maps, and Local History carry the civics side, while World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment, Translation as a Lesson, Heritage Speakers and Family Languages, and Access for Every Student cover language learning and who is included. Geography and Data and Planning and Assessment in These Subjects support the planning end, and a leader or parent would use the same pages to see what checking looks like and how the Thirty Day Move, the simulation rules and the misinformation lab, is meant to run.
